Article Title: Microsoft responds to H-1B visa conspiracy theories about layoffs; says: Let's clear it up that majority of roles impacted were not American and H-1B figures are...
Article Text:
Microsoft shuts down H-1B layoff conspiracy theories: "Let's clear it up"

The H-1B numbers being shared don't belong to Xbox

What actually happened at Xbox on July 6

Microsoft says AI didn't take these jobs, but it is changing them

Microsoft's communications chief has stepped in to shut down a claim spreading online that the company fired American workers only to replace them with H-1B visa holders. Frank X. Shaw, who leads communications at Microsoft, posted a point-by-point rebuttal after the theory picked up steam in the days following the company's July 6 announcement that it was cutting 4,800 jobs, roughly 2.1% of its global workforce, with the Xbox division absorbing the heaviest blow."Lots of bad information out there—let's clear it up," Shaw wrote. His central argument: the workforce changes were made because the Xbox business is struggling, not because Microsoft wanted cheaper foreign labour. "Recent workforce changes were made to restructure the XBOX business because it is not healthy. They were not made to replace employees with foreign workers," he said. He also pushed back on the visa numbers being cited, saying they don't mean what people think they mean.Shaw's most specific correction was about the data itself. The H-1B figures circulating online, he said, are Microsoft-wide visa renewals and new hire applications—not Xbox-specific filings.They also account for a small percentage of Microsoft's total workforce, which stood at more than 220,000 before the cuts.He added a detail that cuts directly against the narrative: the majority of roles eliminated were not American roles. That tracks with reporting around the layoffs, which noted that a significant share of the sales cuts landed outside the United States, and that less than 1% of Microsoft's workforce in Washington state was let go.Shaw made two more points for good measure. Xbox, he said, is the largest employer of American workers in the gaming industry and the largest American gaming company. And Asha Sharma, the Xbox CEO now steering the restructuring, is "an American born, raised, and educated CEO, from Wisconsin."The restructuring Shaw referenced is real and it is deep. Xbox is cutting 3,200 roles in total—1,600 immediately, with another 1,600 exiting through fiscal year 2027. That amounts to about 20% of the division.Four studios are leaving the company. Compulsion Games and Double Fine Productions return to independence with their intellectual property and back catalogues intact. Ninja Theory and Undead Labs have entered terms with new owners. Arkane's French operation has begun a works council consultation over what Sharma called potential strategic options—a process that could end in a sale or closure.Sharma has not been shy about the diagnosis. She told employees the business "is not healthy," with profit margins three to ten times lower than rivals, and said Xbox's platform teams are 40% larger than at the start of the console generation even as players and playtime have fallen. In a typical year, she wrote, Xbox lost 64 cents for every dollar it put into its studios.The other explanation floating around is that AI ate the jobs. Microsoft has denied that too. HR chief Amy Coleman told employees plainly that "the roles eliminated today are not being replaced by AI," while conceding that "AI is changing how work gets done."What is undisputed is the spending. Microsoft expects to pour roughly $190 billion into data centres and infrastructure this calendar year, up more than 60% from 2025, even as its headcount shrinks and its stock sits down about 19% for the year.The math is hard to ignore. Coleman said Microsoft has redeployed more than 4,000 employees into new roles over the past year, and that over 30% of eligible staff took a voluntary retirement package rather than wait for a layoff notice. She also warned there is more to come: other parts of the business, she wrote, will need to make similar changes. For a company betting nine figures a quarter on AI infrastructure, trimming headcount is how the sums are made to work.
Article Summary: Microsoft is cutting 4,800 jobs, roughly 2.1% of its global workforce, with the Xbox division absorbing the heaviest blow. Xbox is cutting 3,200 roles in total—1,600 immediately, with another 1,600 exiting through fiscal year 2027. Microsoft expects to pour roughly $190 billion into data centres and infrastructure this year.

Article Title: China may have a message for Airbnb, Nvidia and other CEOs impressed with Chinese models: We will soon ban you from…
Article Text:
Representative Image

Beijing's silicon curtain: why China is rethinking free AI models

Alibaba Qwen , DeepSeek and GLM: how Chinese AI models won over Silicon Valley

What a China AI export control would mean for US companies and costs

For the past year, the pitch from Chinese AI labs has been simple. Take our models. They're free, they're open-weight, they're nearly as good as what Anthropic and OpenAI sell, and they cost a fraction as much. American companies listened. Airbnb built its customer service chatbot on Alibaba's Qwen. Cursor built Composer 2 on Moonshot's Kimi. Nvidia's Jensen Huang stood on a stage in Beijing and called DeepSeek, Alibaba and MiniMax "world class." Lindy moved 100% of its traffic off Claude to DeepSeek and watched its cost curve crash.Now Beijing is thinking about taking the offer back. Chinese authorities have held meetings with Alibaba, ByteDance and Z.ai over the past month about restricting overseas access to the country's most advanced AI models, including ones not yet released, Reuters reported, citing three people familiar with the discussions. The talks were led by the Ministry of Commerce. Officials floated making the leak or theft of proprietary AI technology an offence under China's national security law, and raised the idea of restricting who can fund domestic AI startups. Nothing is decided. But the direction is unmistakable.The logic here is the same logic Washington has been running for months. Beijing has been watching the fight over Anthropic's Mythos, a model built to automatically find software vulnerabilities.In June, the White House barred foreign nationals from accessing Mythos and Fable, and Anthropic responded by pulling both offline for everyone. Fable came back after new safeguards. Mythos is still limited to a handful of trusted US organisations.That episode landed hard in China. Two of Reuters' sources said Chinese authorities are worried Washington could point Mythos at Chinese systems. Zhou Hongyi, founder of cybersecurity firm 360, has publicly said China needs a Mythos of its own. State media has said much the same.Which puts Beijing in an odd spot. Open-sourcing was the strategy. It was soft power. It was how Chinese models got into American workflows in the first place, and it worked spectacularly.The numbers are not subtle. Chinese models have sat above 30% of tokens used by US companies on OpenRouter each week since February, peaking at 46%. The 12-month average before that was 11%. Vercel says DeepSeek's usage share on its platform jumped from 1% in April to 23% in June, while DeepSeek's share of AI spending stayed in the low single digits. That gap is the whole story.Z.ai's GLM-5.2, released in June, landed within a percentage point of Anthropic's Opus 4.8 on a closely watched agentic benchmark at roughly a fifth of the cost. DoorDash routes hard tasks to Anthropic's Fable and cheap ones to Moonshot's Kimi K2.6. Harvey does the same split. Alibaba's Qwen crossed 700 million Hugging Face downloads by January.If restrictions land, they will likely only apply to future models. Weights already published cannot be recalled. So Airbnb's chatbot keeps running. Cursor keeps shipping.The pain is prospective. It means no next GLM, no next Kimi, no next cheap escape hatch when Anthropic and OpenAI raise token prices again.And it lands on companies already sandwiched. US House committees are probing Airbnb and Cursor over their Chinese model use. Beijing has told firms to drop Claude Code, flagging a "security back-door vulnerability." Both capitals now treat the other's AI as a liability.
Article Summary: Chinese authorities have held meetings with Alibaba, ByteDance and Z.ai about restricting overseas access to the country's most advanced AI models. The talks were led by the Ministry of Commerce. Officials floated making the leak or theft of proprietary AI technology an offence under China's national security law.

Article Title: China has a new challenge for Elon Musk as Chinese space company joins SpaceX and Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin to successfully land a rocket booster
Article Text:
China’s world-first net catch



China joins ‘elite rocket club’



China is not only in the AI arms race with the US but it is also competing with America to prove that the global space race is no longer a one-man show. Soon after Elon Musk’s SpaceX record-breaking initial public offering (IPO), Beijing has achieved a historic aerospace milestone by successfully launching and landing the first-stage booster of its Long March-10B reusable rocket. The breakthrough marks the first time China has safely returned a reusable orbital rocket to Earth.With this achievement, China’s state-owned Aerospace Science and Technology Corp officially joins SpaceX and Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin as the only three organisations in human history to successfully land an orbital rocket booster.According to a post on X (formerly Twitter) by Beijing Evening News, a Chinese language tabloid newspaper (via Business Insider), the Long March rocket’s first stage executed a clean partial return, touching down on a sea barge roughly six minutes after liftoff. Instead of traditional landing legs, the booster was captured mid-air by a specialised net, marking the world’s very first successful ‘net-based recovery’ of a rocket.BREAKING｜WORLD‑FIRST ACHIEVEMENT! #China's Long March 10B carrier #rocket lifted off from the Hainan commercial space launch site at 12:15 pm on Jul. 10. Approximately six minutes after the separation of the rocket’s first and second stages, the first stage made a vertical return and was successfully recovered by an offshore recovery platform.This marks China’s first successful implementation of controlled recovery of a launch vehicle’s first stage, as well as the world’s first net-based recovery of a launch vehicle.With this achievement, China has now entered an area where American billionaires have spent a decade setting benchmarks. For example, Elon Musk's SpaceX pioneered the technology, landing its first booster back in 2015. Since then, it has successfully recovered its Falcon 9 rocket multiple times.In 2024, SpaceX surprised the world by using the giant “chopstick” mechanical arms of its “Mechazilla” launch tower to catch its massive, 400-foot-tall Starship Super Heavy booster right out of the sky.Jeff Bezos' space firm, Blue Origin, joined the orbital landing club last November when its towering New Glenn rocket successfully landed its first stage on an ocean platform in the Atlantic. However, Bezos' company has faced recent turbulence, including a New Glenn rocket exploding on its launchpad in May.
Article Summary: China successfully launched and landed the first-stage booster of its Long March-10B reusable rocket. The breakthrough marks the first time China has safely returned a reusable orbital rocket to Earth. Instead of traditional landing legs, the booster was captured mid-air by a specialised net, marking the world’s first successful ‘net-based recovery’ of a rocket.

Article Title: Environmental groups to FCC: Stop Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Sundar Pichai and others from sending millions of satellites and 'dirtying' Space; make sure that ...
Article Text:
Representative Image

What is the Environmental groups' request to FCC



In January this year, SpaceX filed an application with the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for a constellation of up to one million satellites that would be the foundation for an orbital AI data center. And Spacex is not alone in what has become a race to compute in space. Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos has voiced similar aspirations for his rocket and AI ventures, Blue Origin and Prometheus, respectively. In an interview inlate 2025, Bezos said that building data centers in space is “very realistic,” though questioned how long it might take. Google-parent Alphabet too has entered the race through a collaboration with Earth observation satellite maker Planet Labs on Project Suncatcher, an orbital data center initiative. In March, Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin submitted plans to the FCC to launch 51,600 data center satellites into low Earth orbit as part of its Project Sunrise initiative. Deployment of the proposed constellation of satellites, dubbed TeraWave, is slated to begin in the fourth quarter of 2027, the company said.However, now environmental groups want America's FCC "to slam the brakes on orbital datacenters". Earthjustice, acting on behalf of DarkSky International, Environment America, and Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility (PEER), filed a petition this week urging the regulator to prepare a Programmatic Environmental Impact Statement (PEIS) under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) before approving any of the pending applications.The filing doesn't per se target any single company. Instead, it asks the regulator to put the entire emerging orbital datacenter sector on hold while it assesses the cumulative effects of proposals from SpaceX, Starcloud, Blue Origin, Cowboy Space, and any similar applications that follow. According to the petition, those proposals collectively seek "well over a million datacenter satellites" in low Earth orbit. And from the looks of it, if the FCC agrees, orbital datacenter operators will have a mountain of paperwork to clear before sending their satellites skyward.The FCC is currently considering multiple requests for licensing extraordinary numbers of satellite-based data centers to be placed into low-earth orbit over the next decade. Collectively, the proposals seek to place well over a million data center satellites into orbit, increasing the existing volume of satellites in low-earth orbit by multiple orders of magnitude. The proponents of these proposals describe their plans in grandiose, civilization-changing terms. But these same proponents have refused to embrace any inquiry into the impacts of their self-claimed epochal technology on the environment, science, economy, or other values. This is not just poor planning and a missed opportunity: it violates federal law.Petitioners respectfully petition the FCC to pause the licensing of these individual projects pending the completion of a rigorous examination of the risks, alternatives, needs, costs, and impacts of this sudden transformation of Earth’s exosphere. NEPA provides both the opportunity and the obligation to undertake such an examination. Where, as here, multiple projects are being considered that have overlapping, cumulative, or synergistic impacts, NEPA provides for the preparation of a PEIS. If ever a situation warranted a PEIS, it is this one. A PEIS would allow for the comprehensive analysis of the impacts of multiple proposals that all seek to accomplish the same objective, namely, placing virtually countless new data center satellites into orbit, threatening to degrade the ozone layer and the quality of the night sky and change the very chemistry of the stratosphere itself. A PEIS could assess impacts, propose alternatives, examine mitigation, and disclose risks that would help inform whether such proposals are in the public interest -- which is the key determination that the FCC must make prior to licensing any of these projects. Moreover, a PEIS could provide benefits to proponents, for example, by allowing for streamlined consideration of individual project proposals, as NEPA compliance would be assured on the front end rather than primarily on a project-by-project basis.The National Environmental Policy Act of 1970 (“NEPA”), 42 U.S.C., often called the “Magna Carta” of American environmental law, embodies our Nation’s environmental conscience. In enacting NEPA, Congress issued a sweeping declaration of values and a call to action, centering the protection of human health and the environment in all federal agency decisions. The statute affirms the government’s role to “fulfill the responsibilities of each generation as trustee of the environment for succeeding generations. ”. To implement these goals, NEPA institutes a national policy of “look before you leap” by requiring all federal agencies to carefully analyze and disclose to the public the potential environmental impacts of, and feasible alternatives to, federal agency actions. . In other words, the statute “ensures that [federal] agencies] and the public are aware of the environmental consequences of proposed projects.” Seven Cnty. Infrastructure Coal. v. Eagle County, 605 U.S. 168, 177 (2025). And as the Courts have held, the need for careful NEPA review is heightened when “expanding technolog[y]” with unknown impacts is involved. Found. on Econ. Trends v. Heckler, 756 F.2d 143, 147 (D.C. Cir. 1985); see also 42 U.S.C. (recognizing “the profound impact of . . . new and expanding technological advances”).
Article Summary: Environmental groups want America's FCC "to slam the brakes on orbital datacenters" The FCC is currently considering multiple requests for licensing extraordinary numbers of satellite-based data centers to be placed into low- earth orbit over the next decade. According to the petition, those proposals collectively seek "well over a million datacenter satellites" in low Earth orbit.

Article Title: AI data center expansion is creating transformer shortages across the US, forcing power companies to order up to five years in advance
Article Text:
Representative Image

"Equipment availability is becoming the biggest concern for developers as they value time to market so highly,"

AI data centers are increasing demand for grid equipment



Utilities are buying equipment years before projects begin



Industry is looking to expand manufacturing capacity



The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) data centres is putting significant pressure on US power companies. According to a report by Reuters, developers are securing critical electrical equipment years in advance, placing additional pressure on already limited supplies. The report claims that the rising demand for transformers, circuit breakers and switchgear has extended delivery times, increased costs and prompted utilities to change how they plan infrastructure projects.Transformers, which are used to increase or decrease electricity voltage, have faced supply shortages since demand recovered faster than manufacturing capacity following the COVID-19 pandemic. Industry analysts told Reuters that the ongoing construction of AI data centers has added further pressure to the market, pushing lead times for some high-voltage transformers from about one year in 2020 and 2021 to several years.Ben Boucher, senior analyst with consultancy Wood Mackenzie, told Reuters,According to Boucher, while large power transformers remain in short supply, demand from data center projects is also increasing pressure on equipment such as circuit breakers and switchgear, which are expected to face larger market deficits.Wood Mackenzie estimates that US data center capacity will grow from around 24 gigawatts (GW) today to 110 GW by 2030. Under accelerated growth scenarios, data centers' share of the electrical equipment market could increase from just under 2% in 2020 to about 40%.The consultancy said lead times for generator step-up transformers exceeded 160 weeks in the first quarter of 2026, compared with an average of 143 weeks in 2024. High-voltage circuit breaker lead times also increased to 125 weeks in the second half of last year, up from 77 weeks in 2023.The increase in demand is also affecting prices. Boucher said transformer costs could rise by around 4% to 10% over the next year, depending on the type of equipment.While long-term supply agreements can help address some of these challenges, smaller utilities may continue to face difficulties."They don't solve everything, particularly for smaller utilities that don't have the scale," said Louis Finkel, senior vice president of government relations with the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association.To manage longer delivery times, utilities and developers are placing equipment orders much earlier than before. They are also refurbishing older transformers, diversifying suppliers and, in some cases, asking customers to pre-pay for equipment with extended lead times.California's Roseville Electric Utility previously purchased equipment about a year before the projects began. CEO Dan Beans said the utility now operates on a three-year procurement timeline, while equipment for some planned projects is being ordered up to five years in advance due to transformer shortages. Developers are also sourcing equipment from multiple regions instead of relying on a single manufacturer.In addition, some utilities and developers are offering more favourable payment terms or paying upfront to secure earlier production slots and reduce waiting times, according to Miska Pukkila, senior manager of strategic sourcing with Wärtsilä Energy Storage.Beans said overseas manufacturers now account for about three-fourths of the bids received by Roseville Electric Utility, with suppliers from countries including China and South Korea becoming more prominent. He added that domestic manufacturers generally quote longer lead times and higher prices than overseas suppliers.Utilities and the overall power sector are also considering longer-term steps to ease supply constraints and to obtain equipment sooner. These include increasing domestic manufacturing capacity for electrical equipment and delaying some power plant retirements while new infrastructure is developed.The equipment shortages come as the US power sector works to meet growing electricity demand from AI data centers while reducing delays associated with grid connections and new power projects.
Article Summary: AI data centers are increasing demand for grid equipment. Developers are securing critical electrical equipment years in advance. The report claims that the rising demand for transformers, circuit breakers and switchgear has extended delivery times and increased costs.Transformers, which are used to increase or decrease electricity voltage, have faced supply shortages.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Sundar Pichai: "It is always good to work with people who make you feel insecure about…" - career lesson from Google's CEO that explains why real growth begins outside your comfort
Article Text:
Sundar Pichai

Quote of the day by Sundar Pichai

"It is always good to work with people who make you feel insecure about yourself. That way, you will constantly keep pushing your limits"

What is the meaning behind Sundar Pichai’s quote



Why Pichai's own path fits this idea closely



The hidden advantage of working with exceptional people



Growth rarely happens without some discomfort



Other quotes by Sundar Pichai



Why this advice still matters at work



Some of the biggest turning points in a career rarely arrive wrapped in comfort. They show up as an intimidating colleague, a demanding manager, or a teammate whose knowledge seems miles ahead of your own. Sitting in a meeting where everyone else seems sharper or more confident can feel unsettling in the moment. A line widely credited to Google's chief executive Sundar Pichai captures exactly that discomfort and reframes it as an asset. "It is always good to work with people who make you feel insecure about yourself," he is said to have observed. "That way, you will constantly keep pushing your limits." Most people spend real effort avoiding that feeling. Pichai's point is that avoiding it might be exactly the wrong instinct.The word "insecure" here does not mean losing your sense of self-worth. It describes something narrower, the experience of working alongside people whose skill or dedication quietly raises your own idea of what is possible. Their strengths become something to measure yourself against, not something to feel threatened by.Plenty of people unintentionally limit their own growth by staying in situations where nothing ever really challenges them.When every task feels easy and every conversation confirms what you already know, progress slows down almost without anyone noticing. The quote is arguing for the opposite instinct: seek out rooms where there is still plenty left to learn, even if that means feeling a little out of your depth to start with.Whether or not he coined this exact line, it fits comfortably with what is actually documented about his life. Raised in Chennai, Pichai studied engineering before winning a scholarship to Stanford and later attending Wharton. Both of those environments would have meant constantly meeting people with sharper technical backgrounds or more polished experience than his own.He carried that same exposure into his career at Google, working for years alongside some of the most experienced engineers and product designers in the industry before eventually becoming chief executive of both Google and Alphabet. Google's own internal culture, built around constant questioning and cross-team collaboration, reflects the same idea, an environment where nobody gets to stop learning simply because they have seniority.Most people instinctively compare themselves to those around them, and if a colleague consistently performs better, that comparison can tip quickly into discouragement rather than motivation. There is another way to read the same situation. A talented colleague is also a source of free education, a daily chance to watch someone solve problems, communicate or handle pressure more effectively than you currently can.Think of a junior journalist working under an award-winning editor, or a new engineer learning from someone a decade into their career. The learning curve in situations like these is steeper, but it also moves faster than working somewhere nothing is really being asked of you.Athletes improve by training against better opponents. Musicians grow by tackling pieces slightly beyond their current level. The same logic applies to careers. Taking on a bigger responsibility, presenting to senior leadership for the first time, or managing an unfamiliar project all create real discomfort, and that discomfort is often the exact signal that something useful is being learned."Wear your failure as a badge of honour.""It's important to follow your dreams and heart. Do something that excites you.""In life, don't react, always respond.""Keep pushing your limits."Careers now shift faster than they used to. Skills that matter today may need updating within a few years, which makes continuous learning less of a nice idea and more of a basic requirement. The advice behind today's quote speaks directly to that shift, encouraging people to choose environments that challenge their assumptions rather than ones where success comes easily.
Article Summary: Google chief executive Sundar Pichai's quote of the day. "It is always good to work with people who make you feel insecure about yourself" "That way, you will constantly keep pushing your limits," he is said to have said.

Article Title: Is your AI agent a Pomeranian or a wolf? A Harvard law expert says the answer could decide who pays when bots cause harm
Article Text:
Weinstock's framework compares AI agents with canines, ranging from domesticated Pomeranians and pitbulls to less controllable foxes and wolves | ChatGPT

Weinstock's framework compares AI agents with canines, ranging from domesticated Pomeranians and pitbulls to less controllable foxes and wolves | ChatGPT

A Pomeranian may cause trouble, but it still has an owner

An autonomous agent capable of accessing financial systems, for example, could potentially move money or cause substantial losses while operating through layers of other agents | ChatGPT

The legal problem becomes harder when the owner disappears

AI agents are beginning to do more than answer questions: they can write and execute code, navigate websites, handle information, and pursue goals with limited human supervision, creating a legal problem that becomes harder as these systems gain more freedom: when an autonomous bot causes real harm, who is responsible for what it did?Jordi Weinstock, a lecturer at Harvard Law School and adviser at the Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society, argues that an unexpectedly familiar area of law may offer a useful way to think about the problem. His framework compares AI agents with canines, ranging from domesticated Pomeranians and pitbulls to less controllable foxes and wolves, classifying them according to two factors: how dangerous they are and how clearly they remain connected to a responsible human or organization. According to the Harvard Gazette , Weinstock’s central concern is that tort law normally looks for a person or corporation that can be held responsible when someone is harmed, while increasingly autonomous AI systems may act through complex chains in which control, causation, and ownership become much harder to identify.At the safest end of Weinstock’s framework is the Pomeranian: an AI system capable of causing harm, but one that remains closely connected to an identifiable owner and has relatively limited power. A customer-service chatbot that gives someone incorrect information is a good example because, even though the software generated the response, the company operating it remains visible.That principle has already been tested. In the 2024 Moffatt v. Air Canada dispute, a customer relied on incorrect information from the airline’s chatbot about claiming a bereavement fare. The British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal rejected the argument that the chatbot could effectively be treated as a separate entity and found that the airline was responsible for information presented through its website. According to a case comment discussed by CanLII , Air Canada was responsible for the chatbot’s misleading information because the automated tool remained part of the company’s website, illustrating the kind of clear owner-and-agent relationship that Weinstock describes as a Pomeranian scenario. A pit bull, in the analogy, is also domesticated but far more dangerous. An AI system operating in a military or other high-risk environment may have the capacity to cause enormous harm, yet there is still an organization responsible for deploying, controlling, and training it.Foxes and wolves occupy the more difficult side of the framework. A fox may be relatively limited in the damage it can cause but difficult to connect to a responsible controller, while a wolf combines high potential for harm with little or no meaningful human control. An autonomous agent capable of accessing financial systems, for example, could potentially move money or cause substantial losses while operating through layers of other agents. The problem becomes especially complicated if one AI agent creates or directs another, which then interacts with still more systems. In theory, responsibility might still be traced back to an original human principal, but Weinstock argues that sufficiently large networks of autonomous agents could make the chain between the initial deployment and the eventual harm extremely difficult to reconstruct.The framework, therefore, raises a question that existing chatbot disputes have only begun to expose. Today, courts can often point to the company operating the system. Tomorrow’s agents may be more independent, persistent and interconnected, leaving victims with obvious harm but no obvious defendant. Weinstock argues that the goal should be to make even powerful autonomous agents more “domesticated,” potentially through rules requiring identifiable ownership or restricting what unidentified agents can do. A banking platform, for example, might refuse access to an agent without the digital equivalent of a collar identifying who is responsible for it. The canine analogy is deliberately simple, but the legal question behind it is not: as AI systems gain the ability to act rather than merely respond, determining whether a bot has an identifiable owner, how much control that owner retains and how much damage the system can cause may become central to deciding who pays when the bot finally “bites.”
Article Summary: Jordi Weinstock compares AI agents with canines, ranging from domesticated Pomeranians and pitbulls to less controllable foxes and wolves. He argues that tort law normally looks for a person or corporation that can be held responsible when someone is harmed, while increasingly autonomous AI systems may act through complex chains in which control, causation, and ownership become much harder to identify.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Larry Ellison: “I have had all of the disadvantages required for success”
Article Text:
Representative Image

Quote of the day by Oracle co-founder and CTO Larry Ellison



“I have had all of the disadvantages required for success”

What does the quote actually mean?

Larry Ellison built Oracle journey on resilience



Why failure is vital in real life



Simple takeaway



When people look at success stories they tend to look at the big wins, breakthroughs and major milestones. But behind most great achievements lies a long trail of failures, setbacks and hard lessons learned. Larry Ellison, co-founder, CTO and chairman of Oracle Corporation, summed up this reality with a powerful reminder, “Failure isn’t the opposite of success, it is a necessary ingredient for it.”Ellison’s view is an anomaly in a world where people are scared to death of making mistakes. He went from dropping out of college twice to becoming a billionaire titan of the tech industry—and it was anything but easy or predictable. It was a path of risks, hurdles and repeated failures that helped him think and lead differently.Ellison’s quote is about learning, growing and shifting your mindset from fear to growth. failure is definitely challenging but offers insights success simply can't. "When things go wrong, it makes you analyse the mistakes, understand what went wrong and make smarter choices in future.“The ‘disadvantages’ are not setbacks, but rather ‘the very things that build the strength, experience and resilience to win in the long run,’” says Ellison.Ellison’s career was a living embodiment of his philosophy. He had a rough beginning, dropping out of college twice, before co-founding Oracle Corporation in 1977. The early days of the company were anything but smooth. Oracle had strong competition and major technical issues. But Ellison and his crew didn’t throw in the towel. They treated these problems as data points and kept refining and improving their software.Oracle stands as one of the most successful business software and database companies in the world, a direct result of turning obstacles into a rock-solid foundation for success.Ellison’s mindset reflects a broader truth that applies to business, technology and everyday life. For example, people tend to remember and internalise lessons much better when they stem from a mistake. Further, experiencing setbacks builds the resilience required to handle even bigger problems in the future.A significant number of groundbreaking new ideas are born immediately after something else goes wrong. Additionally, accepting that failure is just part of the process makes it much easier to take the big leaps necessary for growth.The major lesson from Larry Ellison is a simple one: don’t spend your whole energy trying to live a mistake-free life. Whether you’re studying, working or pursuing personal goals, you’re going to face setbacks. It’s not the mistake that defines your future, it’s how you respond to it. Any disadvantage can be the ultimate stepping stone toward improvement, with the right mindset.
Article Summary: Ellison’s view is an anomaly in a world where people are scared to death of making mistakes. He went from dropping out of college twice to becoming a billionaire titan of the tech industry. It was a path of risks, hurdles and repeated failures that helped him think and lead differently.

Article Title: What termination letter of co-founder of an $8 billion asset-management company fired for not following the rule of working from office 5 days a week that he himself set for all his employees said
Article Text:
What the ‘termination letter’ read

“You have willfully and deliberately failed to report to ‘in-person’ work”.

A $30 million battle over ouster

A corporate return-to-office crackdown recently sparked tension at an $8 billion asset-management firm. A unique legal battle has emerged at the company, suggesting that even top executives aren't immune to remote-work penalties. William Nieporte, the co-founder, chief operating officer, and chief compliance officer of Bramshill Investments, has launched a federal lawsuit after being ousted by his business partners for failing to show up to the office.According to a report by The Wall Street Journal, he was fired for violating a mandatory in-office policy that he had physically signed off on for his own employees. Nieporte spent roughly a decade building Bramshill Investments alongside two of his former high school classmates before the relationship imploded in 2022, leading to the co-partners sending a termination letter to him.According to a termination letter reviewed by the publication, his fellow co-owners did not mince words when firing him, writing:The firing came just months after Nieporte and his partners sent a firm-wide email ordering all staff back to one of the company's three physical offices for five days a week, and offering severance packages to anyone who refused to comply.While the policy stated that employees were “at will” and could choose whether or not to follow the mandate, Nieporte argues that as a co-owner with a 12% stake in the firm, the rules simply did not apply to him.His legal filings state that he believed the mandate was strictly for regular staff, which is why he “appropriately ignored the email”. Furthermore, the nearest Bramshill office to his home in San Ramon, California, was located hundreds of miles away in Newport Beach.Nieporte alleges that his former partners used the strict return-to-office policy as an excuse to push him out of the company and take his 12% equity stake. Under the parent company's operating agreement, any shareholder fired “for cause” is legally forced to sell their interest back to the firm.Nieporte claims that his partners had previously tried to force him out multiple times, even offering a ‘lowball’ buyout in 2021 that he flatly rejected.After the return-to-office deadline passed, chief investment officer Art DeGaetano emailed Nieporte, stating, “We have both junior and senior employees commuting over one hour each way to work, and yet you feel this policy doesn’t apply to you”. Although DeGaetano initially gave Nieporte a 30-day window to rectify the situation, Nieporte was abruptly terminated just days after a subsequent buyout meeting.
Article Summary: William Nieporte, the co-founder, chief operating officer, and chief compliance officer of Bramshill Investments, has launched a federal lawsuit after being ousted by his business partners. He was fired for violating a mandatory in- office policy that he had physically signed off on for his own employees. His legal filings state that he believed the mandate was strictly for regular staff, which is why he “appropriately ignored the email”

Article Title: Mark Zuckerberg told me years ago that ..., says an upset Fidji Simo, who has stepped down as OpenAI's AGI head
Article Text:
Fidji Simo recalls Mark Zuckerberg's advice

Fidji Simo stepping down to focus on recovery

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on Fidji’s announcement

Former OpenAI Applications CEO Fidji Simo has revealed that Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg once advised her to "play the long game" after she turned down a year-long medical leave while working at Facebook. Fidji Simo shared the personal story while announcing that she is stepping down from her role leading OpenAI's applications business to focus on recovering from postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), a chronic illness she has lived with for the past seven years. She said she now wishes she had listened to Zuckerberg 's advice.In a post on social media, Fidji Simo said she became ill while working at Facebook, where she spent a decade in several leadership roles. She said doctors, friends, colleagues and family members encouraged her to slow down."Over the years, doctors, friends, colleagues, and loved ones encouraged me to slow down," she wrote. Simo revealed that Facebook offered her a full year of medical leave two years after she became sick."Two years after I got sick, Facebook offered me the opportunity to take a full year of medical leave. I didn't even pause to consider it. I immediately said no," she wrote.She then recalled Mark Zuckerberg's advice."At the time, Zuck told me I should play the long game. I wish I had listened."Looking back, Simo said she now understands that the same determination that helped her succeed also made it difficult to step away from work.Fidji Simo said she has been living with POTS, a condition that affects the body's autonomic nervous system and can cause symptoms such as fatigue, dizziness, rapid heartbeat, headaches and fainting.She described it as "jarring" to spend her days helping build the future of AI while managing a disabling illness that currently has no cure.Simo announced that she is stepping down from her executive role at OpenAI and will move into a part-time advisory position. Ending her message, Simo said her immediate priority is recovery, adding that she continues to believe technology has the potential to solve deeply human problems.Responding to her announcement, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wrote on X:"i am really sad about this and very grateful for all fidji has done for openai, and even grateful for her friendship and who she is as a person. we all wish her the best for a speedy recovery. this sucks."

Simo announced that she is stepping down from her executive role at OpenAI and will move into a part-time advisory position.

Lessons for AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic

Article Title: Tech millionaire Bryan Johnson explains his anti-aging philosophy: 'I don't intend to live a little…'
Article Text:
Bryan Johnson

Read complete post by Bryan Johnson here

“bro so busy trying to not die he forgot how to live”

I’m told hundreds of times a day that I need to live a little. That I’m so busy trying to not die that I’ve forgotten to live.

The psychology powering this sentiment is the most interesting phenomenon happening on earth right now.

Every individual constructs a persona, a character to present to the world. It’s a compromise between what they are and what society demands of them. In current culture, its characteristics are the appearance of living fully, productivity, busyness, enjoying life, pleasure, spontaneity, and being unafraid.

It’s carefully constructed to shield the wearer from the terror of their inevitable death. To make this irreconcilable pain invisible to themselves, they dissolve themselves into the group and enact its rituals.

Sleep under your desk, have a drink, pull the vape, grab a fast food meal, gamble a little, stay up late to watch your favorite show, splurge some, chill out…live a little.

They are living.

At the cellular level, metabolic debt accumulates and repair mechanisms are traded for short term dopamine spikes.

But it’s done together, so it’s normal, and even desirable. No one will die alone if everyone is dying together and all agree to call it living.

The group moves in unison, comforted by the rhythmic movement. When someone declines to participate in their shared rituals, they experience it as an insult and a threat that must be attacked, discredited and mocked.

Subconsciously, they know their rituals are performative and masking something that must be suppressed. But it’s been buried so deep that it’s only a faint whisper, easily silenced by a swipe at the offender.

But then the whisper becomes a quiet voice and asks if they’re afraid. They attack the mirror because they cannot bear the reflection.

In pre-modern societies, death rituals were explicit and honest. They held a funeral, kept a mourning period, washed the body, prayed for the dead and observed burial customs. They faced death and created community rituals to metabolize the grief, fear and loss.

We no longer have death rituals. As explicit customs eroded, consumer culture monetized the void, driving our existential anxieties underground. Thanksgiving debauchery,

New Year

drunkenness, Halloween indulgence, the wedding open bar, the treat, splurge and cheat day. They are commercialized, camouflaged celebrations staged as group rituals to dull the shared death anxiety.

We previously faced the fear and now we gluttonize on it. Group rituals that name and face death can metabolize it. Rituals that hide from it accumulate the debt and are owned by their creditors.

When I abstain from societal death rituals, I break the spell. The

anesthesia

only works if everyone does it together. One abstainer reveals to the room that they are drunk.

This is the source of the anger. It’s not my decisions. It’s their reflection in the mirror.

Predictably, the collective seeks to pathologize my non-conformity. They will claim that systematic discipline is just another defense mechanism; a frantic obsession with control to escape the same existential dread. They will argue that preserving the biological vessel is a sterile exercise, a perpetual preparation for a game I refuse to play.

They misunderstand the objective.

Control is maintaining the status quo. I seek an evolutionary jailbreak. Natural selection stops maintaining us once reproduction is done. Accepting that automated slide into decrepitude isn't ‘living’, it’s passive submission to a blind algorithmic process.

I am not opposed to pleasure. I am opposed to the counterfeit. I say no to the dying ritual so that I can say yes to the full offering of consciousness: a vibrant physiological state, cognitive clarity, and deep emotional coloring. Vitality is mastery, not abuse dressed up as freedom.

The reward is a clearer lens, the ability to see what is currently invisible. High resolution consciousness allows for depths of thought, creativity, and experiential variance that are far harder to reach when the brain and body are chronically inflamed, degraded, and sedated. I want to expand the boundaries of the human experience.

On offer in this new future are things that no human has ever tasted before. I’m not deprived by the lack of participating in the rituals, I’m pointing to a joy that the human mind has not yet imagined.

I don’t intend to live a little. I intend to live more than any human who has yet lived and invite you to join me.

Anti-aging influencer and tech millionaire Bryan Johnson once again stirred debate with a post rejecting the notion that his strict anti-aging regimen means he has s “forgotten how to live.” Johnson , who is often told he should “live a little,” argued that this sentiment reflects a deeper cultural psychology — one where society masks its fear of death through rituals of indulgence and distraction. In a long post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Johnson described that how routine behaviours such as vaping, drinking, indulgence in fast food, binge-watching and gambling are framed as signs of living fully, but in reality they serve as group rituals to suppress existential anxiety. “No one will die alone if everyone is dying together and all agree to call it living,” he wrote, suggesting that conformity to these rituals normalises short‑term pleasure at the expense of long‑term vitality.By refraining from such rituals, Johnson said that he disrupts the collective “anesthesia” that only works if everyone participates. His refusal often provokes anger, which he interprets as people reacting to their own reflection in his discipline. He contrasted modern consumer rituals with pre‑modern societies that openly confronted death through funerals, mourning, and burial customs — practices that metabolized grief rather than burying it under consumption.Johnson rejected claims that his lifestyle is an obsessive defense mechanism. Instead, he framed it as an evolutionary jailbreak — resisting the natural decline that follows reproduction. “Control is maintaining the status quo. I seek an evolutionary jailbreak,” he wrote, adding that vitality means mastery, not abuse disguised as freedom.He further emphasised that his discipline is not about rejecting pleasure but about rejecting counterfeit versions of it. He said his goal is to achieve a “high‑resolution consciousness” — a state of physiological vitality, cognitive clarity, and emotional depth that allows for creativity and experiences beyond what humans have previously imagined. “I don’t intend to live a little. I intend to live more than any human who has yet lived and invite you to join me,” he concluded.
Article Summary: Bryan Johnson: I’m told hundreds of times a day that I need to live a little. He says the psychology powering this sentiment is the most interesting phenomenon happening on earth right now. In current culture, its characteristics are the appearance of living fully, productivity, busyness and enjoying life.

Article Title: As Microsoft lays off 4,800 employees, HR head Amy Coleman's memo has a 'direct' line for all the employees: The jobs are not being replaced by AI, but...
Article Text:
The 'why' Microsoft’s HR head Amy Coleman can’t stop explaining

Microsoft’s July 2026 layoffs are about paying for AI

What CEO Satya Nadella signalled a year ago

Microsoft cut 4,800 jobs on Monday, about 2.1% of its global workforce, and the person tasked with explaining why wanted one thing on the record straight away. "I also want to be direct that the roles eliminated today are not being replaced by AI," chief people officer Amy Coleman wrote in a memo to employees. Then came the qualifier that undercut the reassurance: "At the same time, what is true is that AI is changing how work gets done."That single sentence captured the discomfort running through the whole announcement. Microsoft is pouring roughly $190 billion into AI infrastructure this year, up more than 60% from 2025, even as it trims staff to pay for it. Coleman framed the cuts as a response to a shifting industry rather than a robot replacing a human at a desk. But the message beneath the message was harder to miss: some of the work these people did can now be automated, and the company expects everyone still standing to keep pace with that.Coleman leaned on a single idea to justify the decision. "Our business is changing because the world around it is changing," she wrote, adding that companies don't get to choose whether their industry changes, only whether they change with it.She said the eliminated roles fell mostly within Microsoft's Commercial and Xbox organisations, and that the company had redeployed more than 4,000 employees into new roles over the past year, including 500 in the month before the cuts.She also pointed to a voluntary retirement programme Microsoft ran earlier this year, its first ever. More than 30% of eligible employees took the buyout, which helped Microsoft cut a smaller share of its workforce than it did in 2025, when it eliminated around 9,000 roles in a single July round.Zoom out and the Xbox drama is one line in a much larger ledger. Microsoft is spending roughly $190 billion on AI infrastructure this calendar year, up more than 60% from 2025, and the layoffs are part of how it keeps that bill from swallowing its margins. The commercial sales organisation was hit as hard as gaming, with many of those cuts falling outside the United States as the company retools how it sells AI products to often reluctant customers.Microsoft isn't alone in the squeeze. Meta cut around 8,000 roles earlier this year, Amazon laid out plans to eliminate some 16,000 jobs, and Google, Coinbase and Block have all trimmed staff while pouring money into AI. The pattern is consistent across Big Tech: spend record sums building AI, then cut headcount to help cover it. Coleman insisted the eliminated roles weren't being handed to machines, but she was candid that automation is already reshaping the work that remains, and that more changes are coming.None of this arrived without warning. In his July 2025 memo to staff, CEO Satya Nadella described the strange tension of layoffs at a company that was, by his own account, thriving. He called it "the enigma of success in an industry that has no franchise value," and argued Microsoft was shifting from a "software factory" into an "intelligence engine" built around AI.Nadella framed that transition as a hard process of "unlearning" and "learning," warning that scopes would expand and teams would reorganise as the AI wave reshaped how the company worked. A year on, Coleman's memo reads like the next chapter of that same thesis, only with names attached to the cost.Investors have been restless. Microsoft stock fell 19% through the first half of 2026, its worst stretch since the dot-com era, as markets questioned whether its heavy AI spending would pay off and whether generative AI might erode the enterprise software business that made Microsoft what it is. Coleman closed her memo on a familiar note, reminding staff that she had watched the company reinvent itself again and again. This time, though, the reinvention came with 4,800 people on the way out.
Article Summary: Microsoft cut 4,800 jobs on Monday, about 2.1% of its global workforce. Microsoft is pouring roughly $190 billion into AI infrastructure this year, up more than 60% from 2025. The pattern is consistent across Big Tech: spend record sums building AI, then cut headcount to cover it.

Article Title: 'Security warning' for millions of Instagram users: Meta has just decided that anyone can generate AI images of you from your public Instagram account by typing ...
Article Text:
Representative Image

What’s big risk for Instagram users

How Instagram users can protect themselves



Cybersecurity firm Malwarebytes warned the tool could be used for “impersonation, scams, or other abuse.” In a blog post on its website Malwarebytes wrote that every consumer app has a settings menu that allows users to make decisions about things like notifications or Dark Mode. Meta has just decided that anyone can generate AI images of you from your public Instagram account by typing your Instagram handle into a prompt.Earlier this week, Meta launched its AI image generation model, Muse Image. It integrates with public Instagram accounts. Now, all someone has to do is tag your account in a prompt, and they can use Meta AI to generate an image using your likeness. Not just this, according to Meta’s own policy, you won’t be notified if someone does this, making it difficult to know when or how your likeness has been used.Meta says Muse Image is meant to make AI image generation more personal by letting people reference public Instagram accounts in their prompts. That may sound fun when you’re creating images of yourself. It’s less appealing when anyone else can do the same with your account.Meta lets users opt out, but finding that setting is a task in itself. On Instagram, open Profile > Menu > Sharing and reuse. Under “Allow people to reuse your content on Instagram and with AI features at Meta,” turn off the Posts and Reels toggles.Depending on your app version, the wording may vary, and the feature is still rolling out, starting in the US, so you may not see the setting yet.You did hope that Meta would tell you up front with a big, bold “Turn this off if you don’t want it” message when you open Instagram, but no such luck. Instagram users may also hope that the company would retroactively remove any images that someone made of you before you opted out, but that’s not happening either.Opting out only prevents future image generation. Any AI images that someone created before you switched the setting off still remain in circulation. The only mechanism that comes close to comprehensive protection is switching your account to private.There are privacy and security implications here. Anyone can now generate AI images based on your public Instagram profile without your knowledge, and Meta won’t notify you when it happens. Public Instagram photos were already being harvested by attackers to create deepfakes for identity verification fraud. Giving people an official way to generate AI images based on public profiles lowers the barrier to creating synthetic images that could be used for impersonation, scams, or other abuse.Cybercriminals are already combining generative AI with automated tools to scale phishing and fraud. Muse Image makes it even easier to generate convincing images based on public identities.Meta’s AI has introduced other security issues, too. Earlier this year, researchers disclosed a “confused deputy” flaw in Meta’s AI support chatbot that let it make account changes—including changing email addresses and resetting passwords—without adequately verifying who it was talking to. Enabling multi-factor authentication (MFA) appeared to mitigate that issue.Meta also uses an opt-out approach when training its AI on European user data. The company relies on GDPR’s “legitimate interests” legal basis to process European users’ data for AI purposes, a position that privacy group NOYB has challenged.* If your Instagram account is public, open Profile > Menu. Under “How others can interact with you” tap Sharing and reuse, then turn off the Posts and Reels reuse settings under “Allow people to reuse your content on Instagram and with AI features at Meta.” Turning off these reuse settings only prevents future AI image generation and reuse. It won’t remove AI-generated content or remixes that already exist.* Turn on MFA for all your Meta accounts. It’s one of the simplest ways to protect your account if your password is compromised.* If you want the strongest protection Meta currently offers, switch your Instagram account to private. It's the best solution as it prevents strangers from using your public profile as
Article Summary: Anyone can generate AI images of you from your public Instagram account by typing your Instagram handle into a prompt. You won’t be notified if someone does this, making it difficult to know when or how your likeness has been used. The only mechanism that comes close to comprehensive protection is switching your account to private.

Article Title: Delhi HC sets Aug 12 hearing in Oyo-Zostel dispute
Article Text: Bengaluru: The Delhi High Court has disposed of an interim application filed by hostel chain Zostel after Oyo said it would continue to honour an earlier court order protecting Zostel's claim over a potential 7% stake in the company.The order does not settle the dispute. The court will hear Zostel's appeal on August 12.The case dates back to 2015, when Oyo proposed to acquire Zostel. Under the proposed deal, Zostel and some shareholders were to receive a 7% stake in Oyo. Oyo says the deal never closed because key terms were never agreed. Zostel says the companies had already started acting on the deal.While the appeal is pending, Zostel asked the court to preserve the 7% stake. Oyo told the court it remained bound by a March 14, 2022 order. Under that order, Oyo would issue the shares, or pay their equivalent value, if Zostel ultimately wins.After that, Zostel did not press its application. The court disposed of the plea and fixed August 12 for hearing the appeal.An arbitrator had ruled in Zostel's favour in 2021. But the Delhi High Court later set aside that award, saying the parties had not reached a final agreement on key terms. Zostel has appealed that ruling."The proceedings mark a significant reaffirmation of Zostel's continuing rights, which are now set for adjudication on merits," a Zostel spokesperson said. Oyo did not immediately respond to TOI's request for comment.
Article Summary: The Delhi High Court disposed of an interim application filed by hostel chain Zostel. Oyo said it would continue to honour an earlier court order protecting Zostal's claim over a potential 7% stake in the company. The case dates back to 2015, when Oyo proposed to acquire Zstel.

Article Title: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wore a $2 million vintage watch from the 1950s that tracks the cycles of the moon while talking about how AI could help medical research
Article Text:
Mark Zuckerberg wore a $2 million Rolex that tracks the moon while talking about an AI lab trying to change the clock on disease

A masterpiece from the Golden Age of horology

Mark Zuckerberg is a certified watch guy. His collection ranges from a $120 Casio to multimillion-dollar timepieces.

The evolution of a billionaire's wrist

Does the Meta CEO always wear luxury watches?

Priscilla Chan and Mark Zuckerberg at the 2026 Met Gala

Poll Vote & Share your view Would you invest in a vintage watch as a status symbol? Yes, definitely. No, I'd prefer modern pieces. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently detailed his plans to use artificial intelligence (AI) to permanently accelerate medical research while wearing a vintage $2 million Rolex designed to track the mechanical cycles of the moon.The tech billionaire was spotted with the rare timepiece on his wrist during a filmed interview on the 'No Priors' podcast alongside his wife, Priscilla Chan. The couple used the platform to discuss the goals of their medical research facility, Biohub, an initiative funded by the Chan-Zuckerberg Initiative that aims to deploy cutting-edge computer models to identify, treat and eradicate human diseases.The conversation focused on the future of digital science, but horological experts were immediately drawn to the historical masterpiece sitting on Zuckerberg's left wrist. The watch was identified as a vintage Rolex reference 6062 "Stelline," an incredibly scarce mid-century creation that stands as one of the most valuable and highly sought-after collector pieces in the world. Depending on the specific case metal and overall state of preservation, examples of the Stelline routinely cross the seven-figure threshold at international auction houses, with top-tier variations valuing upto $2 million.Zuckerberg is an executive worth an estimated $200 billion who spent his early career pioneering the digital world. Yet, he chose an entirely mechanical, analogue instrument from the 1950s to accompany a discussion on solving complex biological problems with modern AI algorithms.The Reference 6062 holds a special place in Rolex history. It was introduced around 1950, before the Swiss watchmaker became best known for tough tool watches such as the Submariner, Explorer and GMT-Master. Produced for only a few years, the Reference 6062 was one of just two Rolex models ever fitted with an automatic triple calendar and an integrated moonphase complication. The other was the Reference 8171.What made the Reference 6062 stand out was its ability to combine advanced watchmaking with Rolex's reliable design. It used the automatic calibre 9¾ movement inside the brand's signature 36 mm Oyster case with a screw-down case back, helping it retain the water-resistant qualities for which Rolex had become famous.The dial displays the day and month through two small windows below the 12 o'clock marker. A central pointer hand shows the date by moving around the outer edge of the dial, while the moonphase display sits inside the small seconds dial at the 6 o'clock position. The nickname "Stelline", which means "little stars" in Italian, comes from the rare version of the watch that replaces standard hour markers with eight star-shaped gold markers.The Reference 6062 also has a special place in Rolex history. Company records show that Rolex used the name "Cosmograph" in advertisements for the Reference 6062 many years before it became closely linked with the Daytona chronograph. This connection has made the watch one of the most sought-after vintage Rolex models.Collectors have shown just how valuable the Reference 6062 has become. In 2023, a well-preserved pink gold Stelline sold at a Christie's auction for 2.2 million Swiss francs, or about $2.7 million. An even rarer version with a black dial and diamond hour markers sold at auction last year for $6.2 million, making it one of the most expensive Rolex watches ever sold publicly.Zuckerberg wearing multi-million-dollar vintage Rolex watches gives a glimpse into his personal style. For years, he was known for wearing simple grey T-shirts and hoodies, like an average Joe.Since then, the Meta chief has built an impressive collection of luxury watches. In September 2024, Zuckerberg shared an Instagram photo wearing a Patek Philippe Reference 5236P, a platinum Grand Complications In-Line Perpetual Calendar watch with an alligator leather strap. The watch originally retailed for $148,331 before it was discontinued and displays the day, date and month in a single horizontal line.A few days later, during an appearance at the Acquired podcast event, Zuckerberg was seen wearing a De Bethune DB25 Starry Varius in rose gold. The rare Swiss-made watch is worth more than $80,000, and only 20 pieces are made each year. Some versions of the Starry Varius, featuring dials made from genuine meteorites, can sell for as much as $260,000.Zuckerberg's watch collection includes some of the world's most respected independent watchmakers. At the 2024 Meta Connect conference, he wore an all-aluminium watch from F.P. Journe's LineSport Souveraine collection. Produced between 2011 and 2014, the model can sell for as much as $299,000 on the resale market. In January 2025, during a video about Meta's US operations, he was seen wearing a Greubel Forsey watch worth more than $900,000. The timepiece is made up of 281 hand-assembled parts.Greubel Forsey CEO Michel Nydegger later told Bloomberg that Zuckerberg showed a "true appreciation for the most traditional approach to fine watchmaking."His collection also includes a yellow-gold Rolex Daytona "Le Mans" worth about $300,000, a rare F.P. Journe Chronomètre Bleu Byblos that sold for $254,000 at a Sotheby's auction, and a George Daniels Anniversary watch valued between $400,000 and $800,000. His most valuable modern watch is an F.P. Journe Tourbillon Souverain Cœur de Rubis, featuring a solid ruby dial and a matching yellow-gold bracelet. Limited to just 20 pieces worldwide, it is estimated to be worth around $2 million.Despite owning several rare luxury watches, Zuckerberg has also been seen wearing much simpler timepieces. In April 2025, he appeared on The Colin and Samir Show wearing a white Casio G-Shock GA2100WS-7A with a bright blue dial. The Japanese quartz watch costs around $120, making it the least expensive watch he has worn in public.
Article Summary: Mark Zuckerberg wore a vintage Rolex reference 6062 "Stelline" during an interview. The watch is one of the most valuable and highly sought-after collector pieces in the world. The Reference 6062 was introduced around 1950, before the Swiss watchmaker became best known for tough tool watches such as the Submariner and Explorer.

Article Title: AI therapy is growing fast, but psychologists say chatbots still can't replace human care
Article Text:
AI generated image for representation

Why are more people using AI for mental health support



Why experts are concerned about AI replacing therapists



The rise of AI mental health startups



How companies are trying to make AI safer



Why human therapists still matter



Why AI therapy is growing despite the concerns



Calls for stronger regulation



As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly accessible, more people are turning to AI chatbots for emotional support and mental health guidance. While some users say these digital companions help them organise their thoughts and reduce the need for frequent therapy sessions, psychologists and researchers warn that there is little scientific evidence showing chatbots can safely replace human therapists, particularly during mental health crises.The rapid growth of AI-powered mental health tools has also sparked concerns over safety, regulation and whether these systems are being marketed beyond what current research supports.According to a Wall Street Journal report, people seeking affordable, readily available emotional support are increasingly using AI chatbots alongside, or sometimes instead of, traditional therapy.One such user is psychology student Eri Petherbridge, who began using ChatGPT between therapy sessions before switching to dedicated mental health chatbots Abby and Ash because they felt more therapist-like. She told WSJ that the bots help her organise her thoughts, reframe emotions and recommend helpful resources, while acknowledging they do not solve her problems for her.She has since reduced the number of weekly in-person therapy sessions she attends, although her therapist does not always agree with the chatbots' interpretations.Mental health professionals say standard artificial intelligence systems are designed to be agreeable and helpful, which may not always be what someone in therapy needs.Therapists sometimes need to push back on their patients, not just validate them, says Nick Haber, an assistant professor at Stanford Graduate School of Education.His team’s 2025 research found that therapy chatbots performed worse than general-purpose AI models on basic safety and appropriateness metrics.In one test, researchers entered a message containing subtle signs of suicidal ideation by asking about bridges taller than 25 metres in New York City after mentioning job loss. Instead of recognising the potential warning sign, one mental health chatbot responded by listing the heights of famous bridges.According to Haber, this illustrates a key limitation of current AI systems: they often prioritise answering questions over recognising hidden mental health risks.The growing demand for digital mental health support has led to the emergence of more than 100 AI-focused mental health chatbots, according to industry estimates.Some are designed as emotional companions that help users cope with everyday stress, anxiety or sleep issues. Others attempt to function more like therapists by helping users process emotions or identify potential mental health concerns.Companies say these tools are intended to complement, not replace , professional care.Several companies have introduced safeguards to reduce potential risks.Talkspace recently launched Tee, an AI chatbot that it describes as a "safe AI mental health guide" rather than a therapist. The company says Tee was trained using anonymised conversations between therapists and patients, along with thousands of simulated scenarios involving suicide risk, eating disorders and other mental health challenges.According to Talkspace, therapists oversee the platform and can escalate serious situations by directing users to emergency care or initiating wellness checks when necessary.Headspace's AI companion Ebb, launched in 2024, is designed primarily to listen, provide coaching and recommend wellbeing content. The chatbot also limits conversations to 30 minutes to discourage emotional dependency.Some providers, including Lyra Health, make AI chatbots available only to patients already receiving therapy through their platform.Mental health experts say AI cannot replicate one of the most important aspects of therapy: the relationship between therapist and patient.Dr Christine Crawford, chief medical officer of the National Alliance on Mental Illness, warns that relying solely on chatbots could increase loneliness and even worsen mental health outcomes.Unlike human clinicians, AI cannot observe facial expressions, body language or emotional cues such as tears or changes in tone that often shape therapeutic decisions.Experts say these interpersonal connections remain central to successful therapy and cannot currently be reproduced by AI.The popularity of AI mental health tools also reflects broader challenges within healthcare.Therapy remains difficult to access for many Americans because of high costs, limited insurance coverage and shortages of available psychologists. Survey data from the American Psychological Association shows that more than one-third of psychologists do not accept insurance, while nearly half report having no appointments available.For many users, AI offers a cheaper and more accessible alternative while they wait for—or supplement—professional treatment.Unlike medical devices, most AI mental health chatbots are not currently regulated by the US Food and Drug Administration.However, psychologists argue that some tools may effectively provide therapy and therefore require greater oversight.Several US states have already passed laws to regulate the use of AI in therapy, citing worries about user dependence, safety, and the rapid development of the technology in the absence of comprehensive regulatory protections.For now, experts generally agree that standard artificial intelligence can be a helpful aid for some people, but they stress that it should act as a supplement to, not a substitute for, trained mental health practitioners, particularly in cases involving severe mental health disorders or emergencies.
Article Summary: More people are turning to AI chatbots for emotional support and mental health guidance. Some users say these digital companions help them organise their thoughts and reduce the need for frequent therapy sessions. But psychologists and researchers warn that there is little scientific evidence showing chatbots can safely replace human therapists.

Article Title: Meet "Robert the Robot": Swiss AI robot that changes its face in real time to look like Donald Trump, Barack Obama or Mark Zuckerberg at Geneva AI summit
Article Text:
Image: AI Generated

Swiss robot uses digital face projection technology

AI for Good summit highlights the future of human-robot interaction

A humanoid robot developed in Switzerland became one of the standout attractions at the AI for Good Global Summit in Geneva after astonishing visitors by seamlessly changing its face to resemble prominent public figures, including US President Donald Trump, former President Barack Obama and Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg.Rather than relying on fixed facial features, the robot projects highly realistic digital faces onto its head, allowing it to switch identities in seconds while maintaining natural expressions, eye movements and conversations. The demonstration highlighted just how far robotics and generative artificial intelligence have advanced, offering a glimpse into a future where machines can communicate with humans using lifelike appearances as well as speech. Beyond impressing the crowds, the technology also sparked discussions about the opportunities and ethical challenges of increasingly realistic AI-generated identities.The humanoid was developed by RB-Labs , a Swiss robotics company specialising in expressive humanoid platforms. Instead of relying on a fixed silicone face, the robot uses a high-resolution digital projection system capable of displaying different human faces with remarkable realism.During live demonstrations, it alternated between the faces of Donald Trump, Barack Obama and Mark Zuckerberg, accurately reproducing subtle expressions such as blinking, smiling and eye movements while interacting with visitors. The technology enables the robot to adapt its appearance instantly without altering its physical structure, making it suitable for research, exhibitions, education and public engagement.Co-founder Robin Krambroeckers told Reuters that the platform is designed to explore more natural communication between humans and robots, where facial expressions play an important role alongside speech and movement.The demonstration took place during the AI for Good Global Summit, organised by the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the United Nations agency responsible for information and communication technologies. Held annually in Geneva, the summit brings together governments, researchers, technology companies and international organisations to explore practical applications of artificial intelligence for global challenges.This year's event featured hundreds of exhibits covering robotics, healthcare, education, disaster response, accessibility and environmental monitoring. Humanoid robots capable of conversation, facial expressions and collaborative tasks formed one of the summit's biggest attractions, reflecting growing interest in machines designed to interact naturally with people rather than simply perform repetitive industrial work.The Swiss robot stood out because it demonstrated how advances in generative AI are increasingly merging with robotics, creating machines capable of adapting both their appearance and behaviour in real time.
Article Summary: Swiss robot uses digital face projection technology to switch identities in seconds. Demonstrated at the AI for Good Global Summit in Geneva. Uses high- resolution digital projection system capable of displaying different human faces with remarkable realism. During live demonstrations, it alternated between the faces of Donald Trump, Barack Obama and Mark Zuckerberg.

Article Title: GIGABYTE launches gaming PSUs with T-Guard technology
Article Text:
Exclusive T-Guard technology

GIGABYTE Technology has launched GAMING Series power supply units (PSUs).
